doc.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

chapter: Growing up with jazz in northern England
title: Walking miles to hear Bunk Johnson's Tishomingo Blues
summary: Records were scarce; she and friends including Diz Disley walked miles to a record player, using rose thorn needles, to hear Bunk Johnson.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Were records harder to get in the north of England at the time?

Oh, interestingly enough, there was a guitar/banjo player called Diz Disley in England, and he worked with Stephane Grappelli and he was a great Django devotee. And I remember he had sent for some records from the United States. And one record in particular was Bunk Johnson, the “Tishamingo Blues.” And we wanted a record player to play this record on. And we still used rose needles, rose thorns at the time you know, you used a rose thorn for the record. Did you know that?
Oh, I hadn’t heard about that.

Oh my dear, I can tell you stories. In any case, I remember walking at least — and we discussed this recently, Diz and I — at least five or six miles on a cold winter’s day with a trombone player who had terrible asthma I remember, and he played in sort of the Kid Ory type tailgate trombone between breaths of his asthma, or pants I should say, and we walked miles to go to a house where they had a record player and we could listen to this. And I’ve never forgotten, never ever forgotten. So we were enormously enthusiastic but totally locked into this brief period of jazz you know.
Was the fact that you had to go through that walking and it was hard to get the records, did it make the music that much more valuable to you do you think?

Oh yes I think it did. And I think because it was not so available it was a mission, it was a mission. And you felt that you truly achieved something when you had gotten to that point and my God it was great as you knew it was going to be. I can remember listening to that chorus over and over and over again. I mean it still sticks with me, the
“Tishamingo Blues.” I mean I want to cry, I’m taken back to when I was eleven years old, lo those many fifty odd years whatever. Yes.
